subject: english-literature
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the assessment objectives.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A 'soliloquy' in a play is best defined as...
options: A speech where a character alone on stage reveals their inner thoughts
A short comment to the audience while others are present
questions.explain: In a soliloquy the character is alone and voices private thoughts, letting the audience access their inner mind.

options: The central character whose journey drives the narrative
The character who opposes the hero
questions.explain: The protagonist is the main character at the centre of the action, often in conflict with an antagonist.

questions.q: How does a 'soliloquy' differ from an 'aside'?
options: An aside can only be spoken by the protagonist
A soliloquy is delivered alone; an aside is a brief remark while others are on stage
They are identical in every way
An aside is always longer than a soliloquy
questions.explain: An aside is a quick comment heard only by the audience while other characters remain on stage, whereas a soliloquy is spoken when the character is alone.

questions.q: 'Pathetic fallacy' is a technique in which a writer...
options: Gives weather or nature human emotions to reflect mood
questions.explain: Pathetic fallacy projects human feelings onto the natural world or weather, often mirroring a character's emotional state.

questions.q: Which response best matches what GCSE Assessment Objectives reward?
options: Analysing the writer's methods, their effect on the reader and the writer's intentions
Counting the number of words on a page
questions.explain: Higher marks come from analysing methods, effects on the reader and authorial purpose rather than retelling the story.

questions.q: In a poem, 'enjambment' is when a line runs on into the next without end-stop punctuation. What effect can this create?
options: A repeated sound at the end of lines
A sense of momentum, flow or breathlessness that mirrors meaning
A pause in the middle of a line
A fixed, regular beat in every line
questions.explain: Enjambment carries sense over the line break, often creating flow, urgency or a spilling-over effect that can reflect the poem's content.

questions.q: A 'stanza' is to a poem what a ____ is to prose.
questions.explain: A stanza groups lines into a unit, much as a paragraph groups sentences in prose.

questions.q: To gain marks for using context, you should...
options: List as many dates as possible
Retell the historical period in a separate paragraph
Link relevant context to how it shapes meaning or the reader's response
questions.explain: Context earns credit when it illuminates the text's meaning or effect, not when it is merely recounted as history.

options: Contrasts with another to highlight that character's qualities
questions.explain: A foil's contrasting traits throw another character's qualities into sharper relief.

questions.q: Which sentence best embeds a quotation effectively?
options: Iago warns against jealousy, the 'green-eyed monster', presenting it as a predator that 'mock[s]' its victim.
'Green-eyed monster.' This is about jealousy and it is in the play.
The quote is 'green-eyed monster' which means jealousy.
questions.explain: A good embed weaves the short quotation smoothly into the writer's own sentence and begins to analyse the method.
Iambic pentameter contains five iambs (da-DUM x5), giving roughly ten syllables and a rhythm close to natural speech.

questions.q: A recurring image or idea running through a text is called a...
questions.explain: A motif is a repeated image, object or idea that builds and reinforces a theme across the text.
